body: By twenty past nine the fog over the Lagoon has gone thin, a gauze the sun is working on from the far side. Theo is at the espresso machine in a black cashmere sweater with the sleeves shoved up. The machine woke Jack at five, and Theo has been at it since. The Post-it on its flank is torn down to its bottom half, which still says, in Theo’s neat hand, *+ 1 MALIBU —T.V.*

Jack takes inventory of his half of the closet against Lena’s instructions. Three flannels: red, green, and a blue so faded it’s more of a rumor. No Mooney hoodie; the hoodie lives in 217 now. One navy blazer from the Goodwill on Market Street, for Mass and for Hale. Danny’s Carhartt on the door hook, the Reds moved out of its inside pocket and into his back one. Nothing black. Nothing gold. Nobody in Youngstown has ever dressed for somebody else’s team.

Down in the Anacapa lot, Kevin’s Odyssey is nosed in by the dumpsters, and across its back glass, in white La Vang car-wash polish, it says WHO DAT · TODAY. “She did that at one,” Theo says, without turning around. “I was coming in from the lot. She had a flashlight in her teeth and she was spelling it out loud.”

The Hopkins is squared up on the corner of the desk, where it will stay till October and a mailer. Into the back pocket goes Flannery O’Connor, *A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories*, a Harvest paperback with a spine still white: a Mooney senior-English castoff out of the milk crate. He moves the Benedict holy card over into the first story, where the grandmother is already arguing about the route.

Theo puts an espresso in his hand that he didn’t ask for and looks at the flannel he’s wearing. “Ten a.m. Black and gold. You told me so last night with your coat still on, Costigan, and she wrote it on a minivan with a flashlight in her teeth. In Louisiana that’s a sacrament.”

response: Margot opens on the first knock, dressed, the Moleskine already in her hand; as far as Jack can establish, she doesn’t sleep so much as pause. She takes in the flannel, the stubble, the whole regional problem of him, and comes back from inside with the only thing she owns that isn’t technically a color: black. A Sleater-Kinney T-shirt, washed soft, that fits him across the shoulders like a dare. “It’s from Portland. Return it unwashed and I’ll know.” She picks up her keys. “I’m coming. As an anthropologist.”
Kevin has the Odyssey running in the lot, the La Vang rosary swinging from the mirror. Laney and Lena went ahead at nine to hold a booth.

body: Sully’s is Mission Street’s idea of a sports bar: a green awning, a neon shamrock with one leaf out, a chalkboard on the sidewalk that says NFL SUNDAY TICKET · DOORS 9 AM · BLOODY MARY BAR. A brass band is coming out of it at two minutes to ten in the morning, tuba first, Bourbon Street dropped on a California sidewalk. And on the door, where a bouncer would be if Sully’s ran to one, is Lena Broussard with a fistful of gold beads.

She’s in the black WHO DAT shirt from the fire drill, black jeans and white Keds, hair up off her neck, checking everybody who comes through like the door of a second line. She packed the beads in July, she tells Kevin, “because I am a planner, and the Lord rewards planning.” The music is hers too: her iPod, the owner’s aux cord, a deal she negotiated “until kickoff, and then we’ll see.”

body.text: She stops Jack with one hand flat on his chest and reads the shirt. “That is a riot grrrl band.” “It’s black.” “It’s *Portland*.” She weighs his soul for a second. Then two strands of gold go over his head, and behind him Margot looks pleased in a way she will deny to the grave.

She stops Jack with a fingertip on one cufflink, turns it to the light, turns the other one, looks up at Theo, who is in black cashmere and visibly expecting to be beaded. She doesn’t bead him. “Gold is gold,” she allows, and puts two strands over Jack’s head instead.

She looks at the flannel. Then she puts four strands of beads around his neck, one after another, unhurried, and out of the tote — Laney packed it “for emergencies” — comes a gold sequin shrug, which she works up his arms and settles on his shoulders. “Black and gold, I said. That’s the first quarter. You can earn the flannel back.”

body: Inside it’s one big projection screen and five tube TVs bolted up in the corners, and the room has sorted itself by exile: a Packers table in foam cheese, a Steelers table whose team played Thursday and who came anyway, on principle, and two Raiders guys at the rail who have been arguing with each other since the doors opened. There’s a Bloody Mary bar with a forest of celery. Lena asks the bartender for an Abita root beer. He considers it honestly. “Is that a cheese?” She takes a Coke with lime and a look that means somebody will be getting a letter. Jack gets a Coke, because he’s eighteen and broke and it’s ten in the morning.

Laney has the big corner booth under the projection screen and is dressed for it: gold sequins from collarbone to hip at 10:02 a.m., copper hair tied up in a black ribbon. “Game day in Texas, sugar. This is *daywear*.” Margot slides in across from her in black — “I’m always in uniform” — and opens the Moleskine to a clean page. “I’m here to observe a cult with nachos.” She glances at the bar. “Ritualized masculinity, mediated by a Bloody Mary bar. Hegemonic, but with celery.” She writes that down, and underlines *nachos*.

Kevin, who drove, is in a 49ers cap with the Odyssey key on a carabiner at his belt, ordering fries and waters for the table before anyone can stop him. “Designated adult.” Theo takes the end of the booth. Lena, in off the door to bead the table, points out that he is wearing black. “It’s cashmere,” Theo says. “Cashmere doesn’t take sides. I’m here as a neutral party. Like Switzerland, or Kevin.”
Laney catches Lena by the wrist as she goes by. “Bid Day, sugar. Wear something you can cry in.” “I’m not rushing.” “You’re not rushing. You’re *supporting*.”

At the far end of the bar, alone under the corner TV, a heavy man in his fifties in a Honolulu-blue Barry Sanders jersey is making a plate of eggs last. Lena beaded him at the door. “He’s the enemy,” she tells the booth, “and he’s by himself. Those are two different questions.” She walks Jack down the bar to meet him. “Mr. Dale, this one’s from Ohio. Be gentle, he’s a Browns fan.” The man wipes his hand on a napkin and puts it out, and it’s a hand that has spent a long time on a line. “Dale Wisniewski. Warren.” Jack opens his mouth. “Michigan,” Dale says. “Not the other one.”

body.text: Jack knows the other one. Half an hour up the road from Glenwood Avenue, two fences, a county road. Lena knows it now too. She glances at him, and away, and asks Dale whether he wants hot sauce on those eggs, which he doesn’t, which she takes personally.

Brees walks the Saints down the field like it’s his own driveway, and when they score, the owner, a big pink man in a Sully’s polo, rings the brass ship’s bell over the register, once, a little shyly. Lena is up on the booth seat before it stops swinging. “Sir. That is a *touchdown*.” He rings it again, properly. It is going to be a long morning for that bell.

body: Halftime. The big screen says SAINTS 28 · LIONS 10 in numbers taller than Kevin, and all of Sully’s sits down at once and orders more fries. The owner has rung the bell four times and is rolling his shoulder like a relief pitcher. On the corner TV Adrian Peterson goes through the middle of the Browns again, untouched, and Jack puts his head back against the booth and asks God, out loud and with real feeling, what exactly Cleveland ever did to Him. The Steelers table applauds.

Laney is redoing her face for the second half. Out of a gold clutch the size of a sandwich come a compact, a lip gloss and a gold eyeliner pencil, which she uncaps and aims at her own eyelid. Lena reaches across Kevin and takes it out of her hand. “Laney Price. That is a thirty-dollar pencil.” “Then it’s going to a good cause.” And Lena turns on the booth seat, one knee up on the red vinyl, to face Jack.

“Hold still, Youngstown.” She puts her left hand flat along his jaw to keep his face where she wants it, her fingers still cool from her glass, and sets the pencil on his left cheekbone just under the place where the scar runs out of his eyebrow. It’s cold, and then it isn’t. She works close. Her thumb rests at the corner of his mouth to steady the stroke. She frowns at his face the way she frowns at a Greek participle, and her breath smells of Coke and lime. A stem. A band across it. The curl of one petal, out and down.

Her LG goes off on the table beside the Coke and keeps going, buzz after buzz, walking itself toward the edge. She flips it open with her free hand without taking the other off his jaw, and because his face is exactly where she’s put it, the screen is right under his eyes.

body: Another lands under it before she can close it, all capitals, missing the same letters. Somewhere behind them is the Superdome at half past one, seventy thousand people in black and gold, somebody called Luc, and the boy who held the stepladder in her Mardi Gras pictures, a phone in his fist. Something comes up into her face, quick and bright, and goes. “He’s spelling like Laney,” she says. Laney, who has an opinion about everything, lets that one go by. Lena shuts the phone with her thumb and drops it into the tote, under the beads.

Then she’s back on his face, and finds him looking at her, and her eyes come up off the pencil to meet his from four inches away. “I’m not fine, Costigan,” she says. “I’m *ecstatic*. Note the difference.”

Margot is studying the halftime show with professional interest. Kevin is reading the fries. Theo has his chin on his fist and an expression of total serenity, which is how Jack knows he will be hearing about this until Easter. Laney’s pink BlackBerry comes up over the top of a menu and says it for all of them: a soft fake shutter, no flash.

Lena goes back to the petal. Jack keeps still, and keeping still turns out to be harder physical work than anything the Hobart has asked of him at one in the morning: her palm along his jaw, her thumb at the corner of his mouth, the pencil going round in small cold strokes, her lips parted in concentration a hand’s width from his, and every muscle he owns asking leave to turn his face one inch into her hand, and every one of them told no. Her eyes are on her work. Then, for the space of a breath, they aren’t.

response: He holds through the second petal and the third, and through one more stroke on the left one, which it didn’t need. The corner of her mouth says she knows it. Then she sits back with her head on one side and considers what she’s made. “There,” she says. “Now you’re ours.” She’s turned back to the screen before the teams are even out of the tunnel, the pencil crosswise in her teeth, and his cheekbone is cold where the gold is and warm everywhere else.

Her mouth goes flat with the effort of not rewarding that. “That’s Matthew five,” she says, “and no.” She caps the pencil on the *no* with a click, presses the last curl in with the pad of her thumb, and hands the pencil back across the table to Laney without looking at either of them. The fleur-de-lis is finished whether he likes it or not. He likes it.

She tells him while she finishes it, not looking up. Louis, the saint and the king, and the lilies on the old French flags. Joan of Arc in gold leaf on her horse on Decatur Street. The city flag. The helmets. And after the storm, on every blue-tarp roof and every FEMA trailer parked in front of a house with the waterline still on it: painted on plywood, stuck on bumpers, sprayed on the boards by people who came home to see what was left. She sets the last curl and blows on it once, a cool breath across his cheekbone. “It means home, Costigan,” she says. “It means we came back.”

Dale watches the kid walk off with his helmet in his hand. “The kid’s going to be good,” he says, and goes back to his coffee.

Then the last one: a little screen pass out to the fullback, Heath Evans, who looks honestly surprised to be included and walks it in. Six touchdowns. Lena is standing on the booth seat in her Keds with both arms over her head and the beads swinging.

The corner TV is a different country. Adrian Peterson has spent the morning going through the Browns like a screen door, and at the end it says VIKINGS 34 · BROWNS 20. Somewhere on Glenwood Avenue the radio in the garage is saying the same numbers, low, or it’s off. From here Jack can’t tell which.

Final, forty-five to twenty-seven. The owner puts on his record, Louis Armstrong, scratchy, and Lena lets it play. Then it starts in the booth. Margot does the chant deadpan, every syllable at the same pitch, like a hostage reading a prepared statement. Kevin puts his fingers in his mouth and whistles, perfectly. Theo has the iPhone up, filming: “Week one.” Laney is up on the table in her sequins, against every rule Sully’s has.
Lena turns on the booth seat with the beads still swinging and points at him. “Who dat, Costigan. Say it like you mean it.”

body: He closes the laptop. On the far bed Theo looks up from the MacBook, studies Jack’s face for a while with something like tenderness, and wishes him a very holy Mass.

The nine o’clock is the college Mass, and the college has come to it: standing room under the overturned hull of the ceiling, kids on the side-aisle steps with their knees up, the overheads off and the candles lit, so the blue glass has gone black and the driftwood Christ hangs over the altar in a light that won’t keep still. Three guitars and a cajón. Kenzie Rourke cantors the psalm in a trained soprano that makes the freshmen look up — *I will walk before the Lord, in the land of the living* — and Peter Haddad reads Isaiah from the ambo like a man rehearsing for C-SPAN. *I gave my back to those who beat me, my cheeks to those who plucked my beard; my face I did not shield from buffets and spitting.* Then James: faith without works is dead. Then Mark, and the road to Caesarea Philippi. *But who do you say that I am?*

Lena is two rows up on the aisle in the black mantilla. From where Jack stands at the end of his pew he can see the scalloped edge of the lace and, under it at the nape of her neck, the thin gold chain.

Osei preaches from the step, reading glasses hanging on their cord, and doesn’t take long. “Peter gets the answer right,” he says. “Four verses later, Jesus calls him Satan.” He lets the four verses go by in the quiet. “Same man. Same afternoon. He did not trade him in.” He takes the glasses off. “So bring whichever Peter you brought tonight; that is the one He asked for.” And he sits, and two hundred college students who came braced for twenty minutes are left holding the rest of their attention.

At the sign of peace Lena turns to give it behind her — her hand to a girl in a Sigma Rho sweatshirt, her hand to the boy beside the girl — and her eyes go on past them, back two rows, and find Jack. Then they drop to his left cheekbone, and stop. Her mouth goes in hard at both corners. “Peace be with you,” she tells the Sigma Rho girl with enormous dignity, and faces front.

Through the Lamb of God her shoulders go. She gets the edge of the mantilla up against her mouth and holds it there, and her shoulders keep going, and the boy beside her looks over in real concern, and she nods to him over the lace that she is absolutely fine, *grant us peace*. Jack kneels with everybody else and has no idea what’s wrong with her, and is a little hurt.

Afterward the courtyard empties into the dark of the Grove in twos and threes. The broken sprinkler by the olive tree hisses away in the dark, still broken. Lena is waiting under the olive with the mantilla folded over her arm. Without a word she touches her own cheekbone. Jack puts his hand up to his face, and his fingertips come away gold.

“You received the Body of Christ,” she says, “in my fleur-de-lis.” “All day?” “Since halftime, Costigan. Through Sully’s, the parking lot, Kevin’s mother’s van and the Communion line.” He thinks about the far bed in 412, and the very holy Mass. “Theo watched me walk out the door with it.” “Your roommate,” Lena says, “is a serpent, and I respect him.”

Mrs. Fitch comes across the flagstones in her lavender cardigan with a pink slip held out in front of her: WHILE YOU WERE OUT. “Mr. Costigan. Good. Your grandmother telephoned the rectory this afternoon. From Ohio.” She reads it off the slip, every word, in the voice of a woman reading the parish bulletin. “*Mrs. Carmela Rinaldi, Youngstown. One Mass in thanksgiving for my grandson’s good confession. Ten dollars to follow by mail.*” She looks at him over it. “She asked me to underline *good*. I have underlined it. She also wished to know whether you are eating.”

Osei is coming past toward the rectory with his stole over his arm, the limp a little longer at the end of a Sunday. Mrs. Fitch hands him the slip for the Mass book. He reads it. He looks at Jack over the top of it, perfectly grave. “I can neither confirm nor deny that you have ever been in my confessional, Jack. Your grandmother can confirm it to the state of Ohio.” He folds the slip into his shirt pocket and goes on, and from the dark by the rectory door comes his laugh, once, from the belly, not hidden at all.
Lena was close enough for every word of it. She stands under the olive tree with the mantilla over her arm and looks at him for as long as it takes the broken sprinkler to get through one whole hiss.

body: The marine layer burned off at eleven, and Hollis 302 has its window back: hard blue sea all the way up the glass, one container ship pinned to the horizon, a pelican going by at desk height. The radiator knocks anyway; Yusuf says it’s load-bearing.

Jack is early, in the navy blazer, with the Williams and the Nagel stapled together out of the course packet and Flannery O’Connor riding in his back pocket. There is gold in his left eyebrow. Theo’s face soap got most of the fleur-de-lis off last night; the rest went down into the scar, a fleck of Sully’s that catches when he turns his head.

Yusuf comes in with his water bottle empty on principle, twenty-four days into the fast, and drops into the chair beside him. Before anything else he says, “He called. Yesterday.” Tariq, from Helmand: four minutes on a line that sounded like it was coming through a box fan. “He complained about the food the whole time. Which means he’s fine. When he says the food’s good, I worry.” “Good,” Jack says, and Yusuf nods at the table like they’ve agreed on a measurement.

At 1:01 Lena comes in from the 12:10 with the mantilla still in her hand, folding it down into the OCTAVIA tote on top of the Greek grammar as she sits across the oak from him. Keds. One strand of gold Sully’s beads still on under the cardigan, against the chain. She settles, and skips hello. “God’s cure for snakebite was to make them look at the snake.” “Good afternoon, Broussard.” “Numbers twenty-one. The bronze serpent on the pole. Father Osei in red — very dramatic, you’d have hated how much you liked it. Where were you?” “Reading Nagel.” She takes her own copy out, flattened and flagged in three colors. “Then you looked at the snake too.”

At 1:07 Hale comes in and sets down the roster and nothing else. The linen jacket, and the wine is back on the cuff; whatever happened to last Wednesday’s clean sleeve, it didn’t last the weekend. He stands at the sea window with his hands in his pockets, and there’s a color in his face that isn’t only the broken veins — a man walking into his own house.

“Week three,” he says. “Williams, ‘Moral Luck.’ Nagel, ‘Moral Luck.’ Two very clever men and one very good title between them.” Caleb, who has the Post-its out already and is glowing like a kid in the front pew, can’t hold it. “He wrote his doctorate on this.” “Under the long shadow of a better man,” Hale says, not turning around. “Mr. Hargrove has read my jacket copy.” Caleb glows anyway.

body.text: Then Hale does turn, and finds Jack. “Last week Mr. Costigan informed us that you don’t get out of a thing by forgetting it. This week we find out whether you can get *into* one by accident.” He lets the room wait for it. “Two men drive home from the same party. Only one of them hits anybody.”

body: He gives them the rest of it slowly. The same party. The same number of drinks — four, let’s say; large men, long party. The same road home, the same bend in it, the same dark, the same bad half-second where the wheel goes soft in the hands. In front of the first car there is nothing but road. In front of the second car a child runs out after a ball. “Same men,” Hale says. “Same choices. Same everything, up to a small boy and a red ball, which neither of them ordered. Is the second man worse?”
Jack has the Nagel open to the paragraph and doesn’t need it.

Caleb goes first, because he always goes first. “It’s luck all the way down. Time and chance happeneth to them all. Neither of them’s anything. *Selah*.” Yusuf lifts his head off his arms. “In Islam there’s a word for this,” he says. “*Diya*. You kill somebody by mistake, you owe the family. Blood money. And if you can’t pay it, you fast two months straight.” He considers the empty bottle. “So the second driver owes something the first one doesn’t. I’m on month one by accident.” The table laughs. Yusuf glances down the oak at Jack — the same look he gave him across the lounge on Wednesday night, over *in that room* — and puts his head back down on his arms.
Lena doesn’t raise her hand; she never has. “The same,” she says. “Same sin. Same will, same act, same four drinks. The child is the second man’s grief. It isn’t his sin.”
“Mr. Costigan,” Hale says, “you’re making a face.”

“He’s worse.” He hears the weight on it only once it’s across the table — harder than anything he decided to say, hard enough that the chemistry kid looks up from the highlighter. Lena’s eyes come to him and hold.
Hale looks from one of them to the other, and the pleasure on him is undisguised. “Designated antagonists,” he says. “Ten minutes a round. Win me something.”
She pushes her sleeves up. Both of them, to the elbow, one and then the other.

“Kant,” Lena says, “and I want it in the minutes that I hate agreeing with a Prussian. Even if a stepmotherly nature leaves the good will nothing to work with — even if it never gets a single thing done — *like a jewel, it would still shine by itself, as something that has its full worth in itself*.” She turns a page she doesn’t need to look at. “And if y’all prefer a Dominican: an act gets its moral species from its object, its end and its circumstances. *Prima secundae*, question eighteen. Not from what a four-year-old does next. The second man’s will is exactly as rotten as the first man’s will. Nothing that runs into the road changes what he chose at the bar.” She looks down the oak, past Jack, to Hale. “If a gust of wind can make you a murderer, Professor, then ‘murderer’ is a weather report.”
Caleb says “*Dude*” under his breath, reverently. Hale makes a small mark on the roster.

Jack has the Nagel open and doesn’t look at it. She’s right about the will. He’s known it since her first sentence, and it doesn’t help: the second man still has to drive home past the place where it happened, every day, for the rest of his life, and the first man doesn’t.

choices.text: Every legal system ever gives the second driver years and the first one a fine. All of them wrong?
response: “Hammurabi. Rome. Ohio,” Jack says. “Nobody’s ever been charged with vehicular almost. All of them wrong?”

“All of them *afraid*,” she says, and then — he watches her decide to pay for it — she grants it. The law has to count bodies. It can’t see wills; it only sees what’s lying in the road. “So it punishes what it can find. Put that down as the law’s confession, Costigan, and leave the man out of it.” Behind her Hale uncaps a marker, writes LAW on the whiteboard in letters a foot high, and underlines it twice.

“The man’s the only one in the road,” Jack says. “Nobody in Youngstown ever got sentenced for his will, Broussard. They sentence what he did.” Something crosses her face at *sentenced* and is gone, and she takes the point standing up.

choices.text: “In Youngstown ‘murderer’ is a weather report. Lake-effect.”
response: The table goes up. The San Diego boys laugh in harmony; Yusuf laughs into his sleeve. Lena laughs too, out loud and without apology, and keeps her jewel exactly where it was. “Cute,” she says. “Hold that thought, put a coat on it. Then move, Costigan.” “I am moving. Your jewel’s got no light switch, Broussard. Nobody can see it shine.” “God can,” she says. “He’s the only audience Kant ever needed, and Kant would hate that too.”

choices.text: “I’ll give you the act. Same act.”
response: She wasn’t ready for it. She had the next thing ready — he can see her put it away — and she takes what he’s given her without a flourish. “Well,” she says. “Look at you.” Then, because she can’t entirely help herself: “The act was always mine.”

choices.text: Williams’s lorry driver. Ask him if he feels like a bystander.
response: “Williams,” Jack says. “Ask the lorry driver if he feels like a bystander. He doesn’t, and he shouldn’t. The driver who runs over a kid through no fault of his own feels different from anybody standing on the curb, even the guy in the passenger seat, and Williams says something would be wrong with him if he didn’t. He had his hands on the wheel. That’s a fact about him.”
Hale turns from the window, pleased against his will and not bothering to hide it. “*Agent-regret*. He’s read the footnotes.” Lena: “Regret isn’t guilt.” Jack: “Tell the lorry driver.”

body: Round two she brings Thomas, and she brings him from memory. “*Prima secundae*, question twenty, article five,” she says. “Whether the consequences of an act add to its goodness or its malice.” Her pen taps the oak once per clause. “If they’re foreseen, yes. If they aren’t foreseen — then only if they follow from the act of itself, and in most cases. What follows by accident, and seldom, adds nothing. Not a feather.” She folds her hands. “The child is *per accidens*, Professor.”

Hale, from the window, without turning: “And the drunk who gets home safe? Thomas lets him off?” “Thomas convicts him on the spot,” Lena says. “Same sin, same weight, the minute he takes the keys. The will was bad when he chose it. That’s my whole case, Professor: nobody gets luckier into heaven and nobody gets unluckier into hell. You get there by what you chose.” Her pen taps once more, for the period.
Hale turns his head and raises his eyebrows at Jack: *well?*

choices.text: Read the rest: *per se and in most cases*. It’s what drunk cars do.
response: “*Ut in pluribus*,” Jack says. “A drunk car hitting somebody isn’t an accident. It’s what drunk cars do. Four drinks and a dark bend — you don’t get to call that *seldom*, Broussard. Ask anybody who drives Market Street on a Friday.”

Her eyebrows go up — the best Thomist move he’s made all season, and from the Augustinian side of the table — and for a second she looks like she might actually applaud. Then she turns it around in her hands. “Then the first driver’s a murderer who got lucky.”
“Then he is,” Jack says. “And he ought to lose some sleep over it.”

choices.text: “Aquinas never drove Market Street at closing time.”
response: A laugh around the table, and she rides it. “Aquinas walked from Naples to Paris, Costigan. On foot. In a habit. More than once. He was a big man, and nobody ever offered him a lift.” She waits for the second laugh and gets it. “He knew what roads do to people.”

choices.text: “Miss Broussard walks out of things. Songs. Diners. Maybe if you’re not in the room, it didn’t happen.”
choices.key: In Hale’s seminar you told Lena she walks out of things.
response: It wins the point. He knows it as it leaves him: it’s the kind of sentence that wins rooms. Hale laughs — one bark, delighted with nobody but himself — and says, “Oh, there it is. Somebody’s been keeping notes,” and half the table looks at Lena, because all of them were here the first Monday, when Hale told them about the Anchor.

Lena squares the pages of the Williams against the oak, so the edges agree. Then she squares them again. They already agree. She keeps squaring them. “That’s a fair hit, Mr. Costigan,” she says, very pleasantly, without looking up from the stack.

She leaves his concession where he put it and takes nothing extra off the table on the way past. “He chose the four drinks,” she says. “That’s all he owns. Not the dark, not the bend, not the ball.” A breath. “No. He didn’t choose the kid. Neither did the kid.”

body: Then she stops.

Not the round — she’s still in the round. But the pen goes down on the table, and her sleeves come down to her wrists, and her hand goes up to the medal and holds it, the thin gold oval worn soft between her finger and thumb. She’s looking at him. Not at Hale, not at the table.

body.text: “Then what does he owe, Mr. Costigan?” The formal name stays on, and everything else about the question is gentler than anything she’s said all hour. “If he’s worse. What does he owe, and to whom, and for how long?”
body.else: “Then what does he owe, Costigan?” Quieter. The theater gone out of it. “If he’s worse. What does he owe, and to whom, and for how long?”

body: Caleb’s pen stops over his Post-it. Somewhere down the hall a door shuts, and the whole table hears it.

choices.text: “Everything. He stands up and says ‘I did that.’ Nobody takes it for him.”
choices.key: You said the unlucky driver owes everything — that nobody gets to take it for him.
response: He says it to her and it goes to the whole room. He means every word, and he puts every word of it down on the oak one at a time, brick on brick: he stands up, he says *I did that*, he doesn’t get to go home, nobody — nobody — gets to take it for him.

Nobody laughs. Caleb has stopped writing altogether. Lena’s hand is still at her collar; the point goes past her untouched, and after a moment she looks down at her own pages. Hale has turned all the way around from the window. He looks at Jack without any wit in his face at all, the way he looked at the sea window the first afternoon. Jack finds his palms flat on the oak, pressing, and makes himself lift them.

choices.text: “He owes the mother the truth. The rest isn’t his to pay.”
choices.key: You said the driver owes the child’s mother the truth — and the rest isn’t his to pay.
response: He gives it to her plainly, no flourish. Lena lets go of the medal. She looks at him across the oak, and keeps looking. At the window Hale says, “Hm,” and makes no mark at all.
“That’s the first thing you’ve said all hour I believe,” she says.

choices.text: “Five to ten. Less with good behavior.”
choices.key: You answered Lena’s question with a sentencing joke.
response: The room laughs — the San Diego boys, the Palo Alto girl, Caleb slapping the oak — and it’s a good laugh; it’s timed. Lena lets go of the medal and says, to the table and not to him, “The child doesn’t get good behavior.”
The laugh runs on around her for a while and runs out, and when it has run out she is still looking at him, and he would give a good deal to have the sentence back in his mouth.

choices.text: The Misfit: it never fits. He pays anyway.
choices.key: You answered Lena with the Misfit: it never fits, and he pays anyway.
response: He has it by heart; it’s been riding in his back pocket since Sunday morning. “*I call myself The Misfit because I can’t make what all I done wrong fit what all I gone through in punishment.*” He sets the paperback on the oak. “It never fits. Not for anybody. Too much or too little. He pays anyway, because paying is the only thing he can still do with his hands.”

Hale puts a hand over his eyes. “Flannery O’Connor,” he says, “in my seminar. Someone open a window.” One of the San Diego boys actually gets up and does it, and the room fills with the sound of the surf and the smell of kelp and somebody’s mower down on the Commons.
Lena lets go of the medal. “The Misfit shoots a grandmother,” she says quietly. “Pick a better saint.”

body: Her last move, and the sleeves go back up. She puts both hands flat on her pages and leans into it, and her voice gets that long Gulf roll it gets when she’s building to the end of something.

“Y’all keep saying *luck* like it’s a thing in the world — a fifth guest at the party, with a chair and a name card.” She looks at Caleb, kindly, and then at Hale, not. “There’s no luck, Professor. There’s providence, and there’s mercy, and both drivers need the second one.”

It should be the end of the round. It isn’t, because Hale isn’t refereeing anymore. He comes off the window and stands at the head of the table with his fingertips on the oak, and when he speaks it is very soft and very clear, every consonant cut.
“Forgiven by whom, Miss Broussard? The child is dead. The only one with standing to forgive is the one who can’t.”
The radiator knocks. Lena’s face doesn’t move. Only the color does, high on her cheekbones, and Jack has seen that once before, at the end of the harbor pier, when she said *four days*.
“That’s why it has to be God, Professor,” she says. “He’s the only one who can speak for the dead.”

Hale doesn’t answer. He looks past her, out the sea window, at the ship that hasn’t moved and the water that hasn’t stopped, and the room waits for him, and he goes on looking. Then, without turning his head: “Mr. Costigan. Last word.”

choices.text: “Then why’d He let the kid run out?”
response: “If He’s providence,” Jack says, “He was on that road. Able and not willing, or willing and not able. Pick one.” It’s Hale’s own Tuesday, Epicurus by way of Hume, handed back to him with the bow still on it, and Hale’s mouth moves at one corner.

“Ask Job,” Lena says. “I already beat you with him once, on Ocean Road, and he hasn’t changed his story.” And she gives him the whirlwind like she’s reading it off the inside of her eyelids: “*Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Have you commanded the morning since your days began?*”
“Job got an answer,” Jack says. “The kid’s mother gets a whirlwind.” “She gets the same one Job got,” Lena says. “It’s the only one there is.” She sits back.

She nods once — the nod she gives the end of the Creed, *and the life of the world to come*, settled. Caleb looks back and forth between them as if he’s walked in on a family. Yusuf murmurs, “Factor of safety,” and nobody asks him what he means. Lena says “Amen” to it anyway.

choices.text: “Then the lucky one owes God a thank-you note.”
response: Yusuf, from inside his folded arms: “Certified mail. Return receipt requested.” The table breaks up, and even Hale’s shoulders move once. Lena waits it out without giving an inch. “He owes Him a *life*,” she says. “The note’s extra.”

choices.text: “Is your God the theologian — or the one who pays?”
response: “Last Tuesday,” Jack says, “in Sandoval, the Professor told four hundred people the problem of evil is a bill, and it’s never the theologian who pays it. So which is your God, Broussard? The theologian or the one who pays?”
Hale turns from the window to watch her answer. She doesn’t need long. “He’s the one who pays,” she says. “You wrote it. Page one.” She doesn’t have to look it up. She’s the one who bled on it.

body.text: Hale gives it to Jack, and makes a production of it. “Mr. Costigan has dragged Thomas Aquinas onto Market Street by his habit.” Caleb claps, three times, alone. Three–one on the season, if anybody’s counting, and Jack is. Across the oak Lena packs her pages into the tote without hurrying, and as she stands she says, low, just for him, “You argued that like it was yours.”
He gave her the mother first. The rest of the hour he took off her by force, but not that one, and she slides her chair in without a sound.

There’s no winner. Hale tries to give it to Lena on the last move, and Lena won’t take it. “No,” she says. “He gave me the mother. That was the right one to give me.” Hale throws up his hands. “Two Catholics agreeing about mercy. I’ve lost the room.” Two–one on the season, and a draw, and it feels like more than either.

There’s no winner. Hale tries to give it to Lena on the last move, and Lena won’t take it. “No,” she says. “He gave me every point I was owed and one I wasn’t. I’m not taking a round off that.” Hale throws up his hands. “Two Catholics agreeing about mercy. I’ve lost the room.” Two–one on the season, and a draw, and it feels like more than either.

The room had a lovely time. Caleb is still laughing at something from round two. Hale declines to score it at all. “That wasn’t a disputation,” he says. “That was a revue. I’ll send you both a bill for the hall.” No decision; two–one on the season, still. Lena caps her pen and gives Jack a look that says *next Monday*.

Hale doesn’t make them wait. “Miss Broussard,” he says, “by a weather report.” Lena accepts it with a small nod, no fuss. Two–two on the season. She packs up humming “When the Saints Go Marching In,” under her breath, in the wrong key on purpose.

Hale gives it to Lena. “I enjoyed that more than anything this term,” he says, “and it doesn’t count. A point taken off the person and not the argument goes to the other side. House rules.” Lena takes it, and thanks him, and is courteous to Mr. Costigan in a voice you could chill a bottle in. Two–two on the season, and it doesn’t feel like two of anything. Hale surveys the table with real satisfaction. “Blood on the floor,” he says. “Somebody fetch the spaniel a mop.”

body: “Wednesday,” Hale says to all of them. “Two pages. Prove the thing you least believe you can prove.” He’s back at the window already, his back to the room. Caleb writes it on a Post-it and sticks it to the inside of his *Consolations*. Yusuf says he could prove he’s hungry, and is told that isn’t what the Professor meant.

body.text: Chairs scrape. The San Diego boys go out arguing about tonight’s Chargers game. Lena is gone before Jack has the Nagel in his bag.
body.else: Chairs scrape. The San Diego boys go out arguing about tonight’s Chargers game. Lena goes out ahead, tote on her shoulder, while Jack is still getting the Nagel into his bag.

body: The O’Connor has slid under his chair. By the time he’s fished it out, the room is empty except for him and the radiator and the man at the window. Hale hasn’t turned around. His hands are in his pockets, and the wine on the cuff is the color of an old scab in the afternoon light.
“Do you think the lucky one sleeps, Mr. Costigan?”

response: “No,” Jack says.
Hale stands there with it. Down on the water the ship has finally started to move, so slowly you can only tell by the gap behind it. “No,” Hale says, to the glass.
It’s meant as a joke, and it leaves his mouth as something else.

Hale turns around. He looks at Jack over the top of the empty table — the blazer, the paperback, the gold in the eyebrow — and for a moment he looks his age, and then older than that. “Do you,” he says.
Hale laughs, short and real. “Like a baby, as the senator said, Mr. Costigan. Up every two hours, crying.”
He doesn’t turn around. He lifts one hand off his pocket and moves it, a small Oxford flick toward the door, a waiter dismissed with affection. Jack goes.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps.

body: The Hollis cloister is all red tile and shadow and bougainvillea, the magenta kind with the paper petals, drifting onto the walk and lying there like confetti after somebody else’s wedding. Up on Ferrer Tower the carillon is finishing the half hour, off-key, the Westminster chimes with one bell flat for as long as anyone at Marisol can remember. The stone gives back the heat of the day.

body.text: Lena has waited. She’s at the far end of the walk, under the last arch, the tote on one shoulder and one Ked up on the base of a pillar, and she watches him come the whole length of it.
body.else: Lena hasn’t waited. She’s ahead of him, walking fast in the Keds, and he has to lengthen his stride to catch her halfway down the walk. She lets him catch her, and keeps her pace.

body.text: “You argued that like it was yours, Mr. Costigan,” she says, as if she were reading it off a form.
“I meant it,” she says, first. “In there. That wasn’t a seminar answer, Costigan.”
“You argued that like it was yours,” she says, first.

“You gave me the mother,” she says, first. Then, because the cloister is empty and it’s true: “I wasn’t arguing for the driver in there, Costigan. I was arguing for everybody I love who’s ever going to need the second one.” She looks at him from under the arch. “What were you arguing for?”

“You kept giving me points,” she says, first. “Nobody does that in there.” Then, because the cloister is empty and it’s true: “I wasn’t arguing for the driver, Costigan. I was arguing for everybody I love who’s ever going to need the second one.” She looks at him from under the arch. “What were you arguing for?”

body: A gardener’s blower starts up somewhere past the arch and stops again. Two girls go by with their arms full of rush flyers, and one of them says *Bid Day* like a holy day of obligation. Lena waits for his answer the way she waits for the Gospel, standing.

choices.key: You told Lena the argument was about your brother.

The east stairwell smells of cold concrete and other people’s cigarettes. On the fourth-floor landing the window opens its six inches onto the Lagoon going navy, and if he holds the RAZR up into the top corner of the frame, it finds its bar. Lena’s call is at 8:04, two floors down, every night; he has twenty minutes of stairwell before it’s hers. On Glenwood Avenue it’s twenty to eleven.

Gina answers in a whisper, from under something. He can hear the covers. She whispers the way she texts, all lowercase, and she has clearly been crying earlier and is finished with that and would like that noted.

“it was religion,” she says. “mrs d is doing the corporal works of mercy. she put them on the board like a grocery list. feed the hungry. clothe the naked. visit the imprisoned. and ashley vrabel goes, oh, gina’s the class expert on that one.” A breath under the blanket. “and everybody laughed. even kelsey. kelsey laughed and then looked at me like *sorry* and then laughed again. and mrs d said *ladies*. just ladies. and kept going. we did bury the dead next.”

“Who’s Ashley Vrabel?” “nobody. she does color guard.” The whisper goes hot. “and her dad got a dui last christmas, it was all over st brigid’s, and SHE’S calling ME.” The capitals come through the whisper somehow. Jack has his free hand flat on the cold window frame.

Then, because she’s Gina, she changes the subject in the direction of worse. “dad turned it back on. low. like you said.” The garage arrives whole: the space heater ticking, the radio on the shelf over the Stroh’s fridge, his father in the folding chair with the volume down where nobody could accuse him of listening. “and nonna told the whole altar society you went to confession. she said it like *in california*. like it was fatima. mrs iannucci cried.”

The covers shift. “is the nun real.” “Go to sleep, Gina.” “that’s not a no.” It isn’t. Under the covers, at eleven at night, two thousand four hundred miles east, his sister waits for him to tell her what to do at eight in the morning.

body: The flag out front is back at the top of the pole, snapping in the wind off the harbor as though Friday never happened.

La Flaca came down Mission on the rack on the front of the 11, and on the bus Jack counted the tip share in his lap, behind his backpack: singles, a five gone soft as cloth, quarters out of the jar by the register. He counted it twice. It came out the same both times.
There’s a line of four. Jack waits behind a kid with a cello case who looks like he’s the one being mailed.

The clerk has reading glasses on a cord and a Marisol Little League pin on her vest. “Money order,” he says. “Twenty dollars.” She keys it in. “Twenty-one ten.” He pays in singles and quarters, and she counts it again after him without comment, and the machine prints a United States Postal Service money order for $20.00.

He fills it out at the side counter with the pen on the bead chain. PAY TO: D. KOSTELNIK, in capitals. The address line he does without looking anything up, a street and a number his hand already knows, and then STRUTHERS, OH. On the line that says FROM he writes nothing at all.

The customer stub goes into his wallet, behind his Cardinal Mooney ID. The money order goes into an envelope, the envelope gets a stamp, and it goes through the brass slot marked OUT OF TOWN with a small flat sound.

Later La Flaca carries him down Mission to the wharf, to half-price chowder and the Hobart, and around ten the little TV over the Anchor’s counter shows the replay of the House voting to rebuke the congressman who yelled. Gloria turns it up. Rudy calls an order. Gloria turns it back down. On the steel by the Hobart, Rudy has left him a plate of fries with a fork standing up in them.

That the Lucky Man Owes Nothing

A debt is a relation between two persons, and luck is not a person. Whatever the lucky man has, he borrowed from no one; and what was never lent cannot be owed.

body.title: PHIL 9H · Broussard
body.text:
That There Is Such a Thing as Luck

Providence does not abolish chance; it makes room for it. Aquinas says it would be contrary to providence if nothing in the world happened by chance (*SCG* III.74), because a world without accidents would be a world without secondary causes — no wind, no weather, no free men — and God did not make a clock.

body: Hale is at the sea window when the clock gets to 1:07, as if he’s been there all along. “Williams’s Gauguin,” he says, without turning. “Abandons a wife and five children for Tahiti and paints masterpieces. Williams says he is justified, if he is justified at all, only by succeeding — and he can’t know whether he will succeed until he’s already gone. Had the paintings been bad, he’d merely be a shit with a steamer ticket. Discuss. Mr. Hargrove, I see you’re already vibrating.”

Lena gets there first anyway. “He left a wife and five children, Professor, and gave Tahiti syphilis.” “Miss Broussard has located the clap,” Hale says. “Bravo. And if the paintings are good?” “Then they’re good paintings by a man who owes a woman in Copenhagen five children’s worth of letters.” Caleb comes in for Gauguin fast and a little flushed — the work outlasts the man, the man was never the point, some things are bigger than a family — and keeps going a while after the argument has stopped needing him. Yusuf surfaces long enough to say that right now he would leave his family for a sandwich, and sinks back down.

Jack reads her paper under the edge of the oak while Caleb defends the steamer ticket. It’s very good. By the bottom of page two the providence girl has proved there’s such a thing as luck, cleanly, with Aquinas holding the door for her, and he goes back over it twice looking for the seam and can’t find one. The red pen can wait for tonight.
At the end of the hour the papers go home in each other’s bags, the way they do every Wednesday, to come back bled on by section.
Out on the Hollis steps, in the fog, the RAZR goes twice.

She holds up the pink BlackBerry and plays a voicemail on speaker. A woman’s voice, bright as a stage: “Delaney Rose, it’s your mother. Posture, sweetheart. Posture. Somebody’s earbuds are leaking the new Muse. The windows look west at the Channel Islands, which are out there in the dark somewhere with no moon to find them by.

Kevin has a table by the glass: flashcards in four colors, rubber-banded by chapter, two Red Bulls sweating rings onto a napkin he brought for the purpose, and the maroon quarter-zip with BELLARMINE over the heart. He slides a can across. “Red Bull and shame. The shame’s mine. I got a B-plus on the first one.” He says *B-plus* like a diagnosis.

He warms up with dad jokes, as is his custom. “Why can’t you trust atoms?” “Kevin.” “They make up everything.” Jack puts his forehead on the table. “I had a chemistry joke,” Kevin says, “but all the good ones argon.” “It’s ten-twenty at night.” “That’s why I’m warming up. You don’t go into orgo cold. That’s how people get hurt.” He has a highlighter for every functional group, and he has named the green one Gregory.

Then the cards: nomenclature, chirality, R and S. Jack reads them out in a Youngstown accent that makes Markovnikov sound like a guy with a body shop on Market Street, and Kevin answers every one before he’s finished. Somewhere around stereoisomers, between chapters, Kevin talks about his summer: a Stanford program for pre-meds, and part of it was nights shadowing in a county ER in San Jose with a badge that said OBSERVER, so nobody would hand him anything sharp. Once, for eleven seconds, a resident let him hold a retractor, and he tells it like his First Communion.

“Saturday nights are the worst,” he says, sunny, squaring a stack. “There was one in July. Two cars on Story Road. A minivan, a family, the dad driving, and a guy in a pickup who’d been at a barbecue since noon.” He snaps a rubber band around the stack. “They worked on the dad a long time. The little girl was okay. The guy in the pickup came in walking and sat in a chair in the hall and kept asking the nurses was he in trouble.” He looks out at the dark where the islands are.
Jack finds his own thumb on the scar through his eyebrow. Kevin, who is going to be a doctor, notices, and the smile comes back on. “What happened there, anyway?”

Theo comes back from the showers down the hall in a towel, wet hair pushed back, his things in a leather case that has been to more countries than Jack has. “You have anything that fits a RAZR?” “Top shelf. The gray bag.” Theo points with his chin. “It’s in with the camera stuff. The Canon takes the same cable — mini-USB. It’s the only thing your phone and my camera have in common, Costigan. Treasure it.”

There are two bags on the top shelf of the closet. Jack goes up on his toes and pulls the one in front, the black one, because it’s in front: heavier than he expects, the zipper open halfway. He reaches in for a cable and comes out with denim.

A jacket. A women’s Levi’s jacket, small, the cuffs worn soft. He shakes it out to see what it is, and as it unfolds the back swings toward him, and on the back is Our Lady of Guadalupe, embroidered, a hand’s span tall: the blue-green mantle with its stars, the gold rays all around her, roses at her feet. Stitched by hand. He can see where the thread was knotted.
Theo crosses the room — it’s the fastest Jack has seen him move all week — and takes it out of his hands.

“A girl left it.” He’s already folding it, sleeves in, the back turned to the inside. “Brentwood girl. Marymount. She’s in Prague for the semester; she left it in the car, and I keep meaning to mail it to her. Nobody has an address in Prague. Have you ever tried to get an address in Prague? It’s all *ulice* this and *náměstí* that, and the post office is a palace, and the palace is closed.” The jacket goes into the black bag and the bag gets zipped, all the way, and Theo puts it back on the shelf himself, at the back. He takes down the gray one, finds the cable in a side pocket, and hands it over. “There. Mini-USB. A miracle of standardization.”
He gets into bed with the MacBook and his headphones on, and the menu screen of whatever it is lights his face blue and goes on looping, nothing playing.

“I’m going to.” Theo settles the headphones. After a while, on his side of the room, the movie starts.

Before Evan can open the book, Lena says it. “We read it. ‘Our Duty to Love the People We See.’ It was good.” Evan looks at her as if she’d spoken in a language he grew up in and hasn’t heard in years. He takes a moment before he nods. Then he closes the book on the desk.

They talk about Hale instead, because everyone does. This morning in Sandoval 1 Hale gave the four hundred the two drivers, slower and meaner than he gave them to the seminar, and finished on a line Jack wrote on the back flyleaf of the O’Connor: *The bill arrives at the wrong address. It always has.* The girl in the Marisol Surf hoodie wants to know if that means the one who hit the kid is worse or just, like, sadder. The Sigma Rho kid, visor backward, says it’s all luck, bro, you get pulled over or you don’t, and then hears himself and adds, “I mean morally.” Somebody asks whether Evan is going to tell them what Kierkegaard thinks, and Evan says Kierkegaard thinks they should stop asking what Kierkegaard thinks. Lena says the one who hit the kid is worse *off*, not worse, and that those are different words for a reason; the Marisol Surf girl writes *worse off* on the back of her hand. Evan lets them go around twice.
Then, looking at the window rather than at any of them: “You’ve left out a driver. The one who stops, looks, sees nothing, and drives home.”

body: She has the Moleskine out for the follow-up, and on the porch an active in a headset, with a clipboard of her own, has been glaring at her across Seacliff for ten minutes with a pure, professional hatred. Margot looks right back, and writes the glare down.

Lena is at the other end of the bench, in a blue sundress with small white flowers on it — “I can cry in this one, I tested it” — and her mascara, she wants him to know, is waterproof. “Laney said wear something you can cry in. I extended it to the face.” She has her boots planted and her hands knotted in her lap, and she is watching the top of the road as if something is coming in off the Gulf.

At nine minutes past five a whoop goes up from the far end of Seacliff and the new members come down the road at a dead run: sixty girls in matching pink T-shirts that say PI LAM RODEO, bandanas at their throats, cowboy hats, boots that have never been introduced to a horse. Laney, who is from Texas, will be telling everyone who holds still, for the rest of the semester, that the theme is cultural theft. She is out in front anyway in a pink straw cowboy hat, copper hair coming loose behind her. On the porch steps Sloane Kittredge has the clipboard and is calling names like a ring announcer.

Laney hits the porch and screams, and is screamed at, and screams back, and is passed hand to hand across a crush of white dresses — and then she turns around, finds the bench, and comes straight back across Seacliff at a sprint in wedge heels, through a gap between a Jetta and a surf van, holding the hat on with one hand. She goes into Lena first. They’re both crying at once, Lena’s waterproof holding up, Laney’s not, Laney saying “I *know*, I *know*” into Lena’s hair as though Lena had said anything. Then she lets go and gets Jack around the neck. “FIREMAN.”

body.text: Into his collar, quieter, before she lets go: “You stayed till I slept.”

body: Margot has the pen up. “On the record?” Laney puts the hat back on and squares it. “Sugar, I *am* the record.” Two actives come across the road and take her back by the elbows, lifeguards bringing in a swimmer who didn’t want saving, and Laney goes, waving over her shoulder with the hand that isn’t holding her hat on.

Lena watches her go with the heels of both hands under her eyes. “She ran to me first,” she says, to the bench in general. “In front of Sloane Kittredge and the whole chapter. Did y’all see that?” Margot, writing: “Observed.” “Nobody runs back across the road. You get your hat and your sisters and you go in.” She sits back down on the bench. “She’s going to be insufferable,” she says, with enormous satisfaction.
Behind them a champagne-gold convertible comes down Seacliff slow with the top down. Theo lifts one hand off the wheel without turning his head, and keeps going west.

Above him, against the sky, there’s the bench and a shape on it with its hands in its lap.

“*Professor.*” His brother, out of breath, a room full of men behind him and a steel door somewhere that buzzes and slams. “Got your letter. *Sixty-six degrees. Green on top and gray underneath.* I read it to Reggie in the next bunk. Reggie’s from Portsmouth. Never seen nothing bigger than the Ohio River. He wants to know does it smell.” “Like kelp.” “I don’t know what that is, Professor, and neither does Reggie.”

A pause with a television in it. “You never write when there’s nothing to say. Somebody tell you to?” Jack watches a gull walk off with something it shouldn’t have. “A guy at work.” “Tell him thanks.” The book is in the mailroom, Danny says; they read it before he does, and some C.O. is finding out how it ends on his lunch break. Up on the road the porch hits the chorus, sixty women screaming at the sky, and it comes right down the bluff. “Where are you, a zoo?” “Sorority thing.” “*Professor.*”

“Called the house last night,” Danny says, a step quieter. “Gina picked up. Said everything’s fine, which is how I know it ain’t. She’s been saying fine since she was four.” He waits. “You know something.”

Up on the road nobody can hear him. Down here there’s nobody but the gulls. So Jack tells him: religion class, the corporal works of mercy up on the board like a grocery list, *visit the imprisoned*, Ashley Vrabel, everybody laughing, Mrs. D saying *ladies* and going on to bury the dead.
For a while there’s only the television on Danny’s end, and somebody laughing at it.
“The class expert,” Danny says finally. “On me.” A breath that doesn’t go all the way in. “She shouldn’t have to carry me to school, Professor. She’s fifteen.” Then, harder: “What’d you tell her?”

body.text: “To say your name. Just ‘Danny.’ Then look at the girl till she looks away.” Nothing on the line. Then: “My name,” Danny says. “Okay. Yeah. Okay.”

“To ask the girl how her dad’s DUI is going.” Danny laughs, one bark, loud enough that somebody on his end tells him to shut up. Then, quieter: “Tell her don’t. She’s better than the Vrabels. Somebody in this family’s got to be.”
“That she gets to be your sister anyway.” Nothing on the line. “Yeah,” Danny says, rough. “Yeah. She does.”
“To tell Ma.” “Good.” Danny almost laughs. “Mrs. D’s never seen Ma in her work shoes.”

body: “Tell her she did good,” Danny says. “Going back in the next day. That’s the hard part, Professor. Tell her I said.” “I’ll tell her.”
Then, quick, getting the important thing in before the money runs out: “Hey. Is the veil girl there?”
Jack looks up the stairs at the bench.

body.text: “Hold on,” Danny says. “Say something else.” “Something else,” Lena says, and on the line there’s a pause while he listens. “You’re the New Orleans one. I can hear it from here. He says you argue like a prosecutor” — loud enough for Jack to hear his own letter from two weeks ago coming back to him through a prison phone. Lena sits up straighter on the bench. “Defense, actually,” she says. “I’m going to be defense.” And Danny laughs, and it’s the old one, the one from the driveway on Glenwood with his head under the hood of somebody’s Buick, the one Jack had stopped expecting to hear again. Jack has to look at the sea for a while. “Gina says Nonna’s got you down as a nun,” Danny says. “Your grandmother,” Lena tells him, “has been misinformed.” She listens to something that makes her smile at her own knees. Then she hands the phone back, warm. “The *veil girl*.” She lets him suffer exactly one second. “I’ve been called worse in Latin.”
“Tell her I said hey,” Danny says again, in case it didn’t take. “And next time you take a girl to a zoo, Professor, you buy her a pretzel. Ma raised you.”

body: Then the recorded woman, right on top of him: “You have one minute remaining.” Danny talks faster. “Professor, listen — tell Gina — ”
Click.
Not even the dial tone yet: a click, and then a hiss, and then nothing at all. Across the road the porch is still playing Beyoncé.

body.text: Jack sits on the landing with the dead phone until a gull lands on the rail and looks at him. Then he climbs. Lena watches him come up the last flight. “He says hey,” Jack says, and Lena says “Hey” back, very quietly, out toward the water, as if it might get there. “He got cut off. ‘Tell Gina — ’ and then the machine.”
“Tell Gina what?” Lena says. “I don’t know.” “Then you ask him next time, Jack.” It’s the first time she’s said his name since the olive tree.
“Tell Gina what?” Lena says. “I don’t know.” “Then you ask him next time, Mr. Costigan.” She says the *Mr.* more gently than she has all week, but she says it.

body: She doesn’t touch him. She sits with him while the sun gets lower over the water and the porch runs through its handful of songs again from the top — forty women groaning at the first bars of “Single Ladies” and singing every word anyway — the two of them watching the girls in pink hats go in and out of the front door, until it’s twenty past six and he has to go get La Flaca off the rack and ride to the Anchor for his Thursday shift. When he stands, she lifts a hand from her lap — go, ride safe — and stays where she is, watching the porch.

journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. s14.slug: FRIDAY · 2:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The Thursday shift lets him go at twenty past one. Tonight Gloria rated a long-haul trucker to his face, *lemon meringue — all air*, and the trucker tipped her five dollars for it. At midnight Rudy put a plate of eggs on the steel by the Hobart and pointed at it with the spatula until the dish man ate. At close Gloria made him take the last slice of the lemon meringue home in foil, “for the ride,” and it’s in La Flaca’s basket now, all air. The RAZR charger came out from behind the machine furred with lint and smelling of bleach, and it’s coiled in his back pocket beside the O’Connor. La Flaca got him up Mission and out Ocean Road in the cold, her coaster brakes complaining at every grade.

Delgado at ten past two. Through the lobby glass Marcus is asleep at the front desk again, organic chemistry this week, rising and falling on his chest. Jack sits down on the front steps instead of going in. The gold went down the drain on Tuesday — the last fleck of it came out of his eyebrow in the fourth-floor shower — and his face is just his face.
*Do you think the lucky one sleeps, Mr. Costigan?* He’s had four nights to come up with a better answer than the one he gave in Hollis 302. He’s still working on it.

At 2:10 the horn comes up off the bluff. Two long, one short, one long: the long notes low and patient, the short one a hitch in the middle, the last held out over the water until the fog takes the end of it. Then the freight itself, steel on steel down in the dark below the Lagoon, and the concrete step under him taking a share of the weight. Jack counts under his breath, the way he has since he was six, one car into the next, alone this time. The twenties. The forties. The sound goes on up the coast and thins and is gone.
Sixty.
At 2:14 the RAZR goes in his pocket.

s14b.slug: FRIDAY · 2:16 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He goes in. Marcus doesn’t wake; organic chemistry goes up and down. The elevator takes its time getting to four. The lounge is dark, the whiteboard a pale square on the far wall, and under the door of 412 there’s no light at all, Theo’s screen off, Theo a long shape under the comforter. Jack doesn’t turn on the lamp. He sets the O’Connor on the desk beside the Hopkins, and lays the RAZR next to them, open to her text, and lies down on top of the blanket in his clothes. The screen keeps her lit for the fifteen seconds it’s allowed — *Goodnight, Jack. —L.* — and then it goes dark, and he lies there with his eyes open, listening to the building breathe.
